client: I've been really struggling lately with anxiety about my final exams coming up, and it got a lot worse after I got a low grade on my last psychology paper. It's like this constant knot in my stomach that won't go away, and I keep telling myself that if I failed that paper, I'm probably going to fail the finals too. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of heaviness right now, and that constant knot in your stomach makes complete sense given the pressure you're feeling around exams. I'm really glad you decided to give this a shot, even with some doubt about whether it'll help — that kind of courage matters. I'd love to gently explore that thought you mentioned, that one low grade *means* you'll fail the finals — what evidence do you have that that's actually true, and is there anything that might point in a different direction?

client: I mean, I guess the evidence I have is just... that grade. It was really bad, like a D, and I've never gotten anything that low before, so it just feels like a sign that I don't understand the material at all. But I know part of me is aware that I've done okay in other classes this semester, so maybe it's not a complete picture, but it's hard to hold onto that when the anxiety is so loud.
therapist: It's really insightful that you can already see the bigger picture — that one difficult grade exists alongside a semester where you've actually been doing okay in other areas — even when the anxiety is making it hard to hold onto that truth. What you're describing is something we call "tunnel vision," where our anxious mind zooms in on the one piece of evidence that confirms our fear and pushes the rest out of frame. What do you think it would mean about you as a student if you held *both* pieces of evidence equally — the D *and* the classes where you've done well?

client: I guess if I held both equally, it would mean I'm a student who's mostly managing but hit a rough patch with one assignment, which... actually sounds a lot less catastrophic when I say it out loud. But honestly, it's hard for me to really believe that, because the voice in my head keeps saying that the D is the "real" truth and the other grades are just flukes. It's like I automatically trust the bad evidence more than the good, and I don't really know how to change that pattern.
therapist: You've just made a really important observation about yourself — noticing that you automatically trust the negative evidence more than the positive is actually a huge step, because you can't change a pattern you haven't seen yet. This tendency has a name in CBT: "negative filtering," and the fact that you named it so clearly suggests your rational mind is stronger than that anxious voice gives it credit for. What do you think that inner voice is trying to protect you from — is there something it's afraid would happen if you actually let yourself believe the more balanced version?

client: That's actually a really interesting question, and I think the voice is afraid that if I relax and believe things are okay, I'll stop trying hard enough and then actually fail. Like, the anxiety almost feels necessary, as if it's the only thing keeping me from completely falling apart or getting complacent. But I can also see how that's kind of exhausting and maybe not even working, because I've been anxious this whole semester and that paper still went badly.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really profound — the idea that anxiety is your "engine" keeping you from failure, which makes it feel dangerous to let go of, even when it's exhausting you. But you've already spotted the crack in that belief yourself: the anxiety was there all semester, and it didn't actually prevent that difficult grade, which suggests it might be more of a burden than a safety net. What might a gentler form of motivation look like for you — one that keeps you engaged and working hard without the constant knot in your stomach?

client: I want to say something like studying because I actually find the subject interesting, or because I want to understand the material rather than just survive the exam, but honestly that feels kind of naive or idealistic right now. Like, I'm not sure I even remember what it feels like to be curious about psychology without the fear attached to it, because the anxiety has been there for so long. I guess I'm also a little skeptical that just shifting my motivation is something I can actually do when finals are weeks away and the pressure is already so real.
therapist: What you're describing — that flicker of remembering curiosity-driven learning, even if it feels distant right now — is actually really meaningful, and it's not naive at all; it's pointing toward something that was real for you before the anxiety took over. You're right that completely rewiring your motivation before finals isn't realistic, and I don't want to offer you something that feels hollow, but even small moments of genuine interest alongside the pressure can start to loosen anxiety's grip a little. Can you think of a time, even briefly this semester, when you were engaged with psychology material because it genuinely interested you rather than out of fear?

client: Actually, yeah, there was this one lecture about cognitive dissonance that I remember genuinely getting excited about, because it connected to something I'd noticed in my own life and I kept thinking about it even after class. But then the next assignment came back with a bad comment from the professor and that excitement just kind of got buried. I guess I didn't realize until right now that the curiosity was there before the fear showed up and smothered it.
therapist: That moment with cognitive dissonance is really precious — it shows that the curiosity isn't gone, it's just been buried under layers of fear and self-doubt, and you just dug it back up a little right now in this conversation. It's also so telling that the excitement was there *first*, before the professor's comment arrived and covered it over, which means anxiety isn't your natural state with psychology — it's something that got layered on top. What do you think it would take, even in a small way, to let that cognitive dissonance curiosity — or something like it — have a little space alongside the exam pressure in the weeks ahead?

client: Maybe I could try to find one thing in my study material that genuinely interests me and let myself sit with that for a few minutes before switching into panic-revision mode, but I'm worried that once I open my notes the anxiety will just take over and the curiosity won't stand a chance. It's like I can see the idea working in theory, but in practice the fear feels so much louder and more immediate than any curiosity. I guess I'm not sure how to protect that small space of interest when the pressure is constantly crowding it out.
therapist: You've actually just designed a really thoughtful, concrete experiment for yourself — finding one genuinely interesting thread before shifting into revision mode — and the fact that you can envision it so clearly suggests it's more achievable than the fear is telling you right now. One thing that might help protect that small space is treating it like a brief ritual with a defined boundary, even just two or three minutes where you give yourself explicit permission to be curious before the exam-focused work begins, which can make it feel less like the anxiety is "winning" if it shows up afterward. What would make that tiny window feel safe enough to actually try — is there a specific time, place, or even a particular topic you could imagine starting with this week?

client: I think maybe mornings could work, before I've had time to spiral, and I could start with something related to that cognitive dissonance topic since it already has some good feeling attached to it. But I'm a little worried that if I try this and the anxiety crashes in anyway, I'll just see it as proof that nothing works and feel even worse than before. I guess I'm asking, what do I do if I try the two minutes and it just doesn't feel curious at all, it just feels like more pressure?
therapist: Mornings with cognitive dissonance sounds like a genuinely wise starting point, and I love that you're already thinking ahead to protect the experiment from becoming another way to judge yourself. The key reframe here is that even if anxiety shows up during those two minutes, that's not proof the experiment failed — it's just useful information, because you're not trying to eliminate anxiety, you're practicing making a small space for curiosity *alongside* it, and that takes repetition before it feels natural. What if, instead of measuring success by how curious you felt, you measured it simply by whether you showed up and tried — would that feel like a safer way to give this a chance?

client: Measuring it by whether I showed up rather than how I felt actually does take some pressure off, and I can see how that might stop me from turning it into another thing to fail at. But I guess I'm a little suspicious of myself, because I have a history of committing to things like this and then quietly dropping them after a few days when life gets busy or the anxiety feels too big. How do I keep this from just becoming another good intention that fades out before the finals even arrive?
therapist: It's really honest and self-aware of you to name that pattern rather than just hoping this time will be different, and that kind of self-knowledge is actually an asset here, not a flaw. One thing that helps in CBT is making the commitment as small and specific as possible — "two minutes with cognitive dissonance on Monday morning before coffee" is much harder to quietly drop than a vague intention, because it's concrete enough that you'll notice when you've skipped it. Who in your life, or what small reminder system, could act as a gentle external anchor to help you follow through when your own motivation gets crowded out by the busy days ahead?

client: Honestly, the external anchor idea makes me a little uncomfortable, because I don't really have many people I feel close enough to ask something like that without it feeling embarrassing or like I'm burdening them. I'm pretty isolated when it comes to the exam stress, like most of my friends seem to be handling things fine and I don't want them to see how much I'm struggling. Maybe a phone reminder could work, but I've ignored those before, so I'm not totally confident that's enough to actually hold me accountable.
therapist: There's something quietly painful in what you just shared — that sense of being isolated with this struggle while everyone around you seems to be coping fine — and I want to gently name that the belief that you'd be a burden might be worth examining the same way we looked at the exam evidence, because it's possible your friends would feel closer to you, not burdened, if they knew. But I also hear that you're not ready for that right now, and that's okay — what might make a phone reminder feel more meaningful than ones you've ignored before, like a specific message to yourself that captures why this small experiment actually matters to you?
